A day of rallies, tributes and fanfare as BNP makes November 7 historic again
item.description:
The Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) observed National Revolution and Solidarity Day with rallies and programs across the country on Saturday, marking the occasion for the first time with state-level celebrations since returning to power.
The BNP-led government declared November 7 a public holiday and organised official programs to commemorate the historic events of 1975.
In Dhaka, Prime Minister and BNP Chairman Tarique Rahman led a nearly six-kilometre procession from Nayapaltan to Manik Mia Avenue, marking the 51st anniversary of the day.
Photo: Ahadul Karim Khan/Dhaka Tribune
The procession, titled “National Revolution and Solidarity Day Sovereignty Rally”, began around 3:30pm from in front of the BNP's central office after a brief speech by Tarique. It reached Manik Mia Avenue around an hour later, passing through several major roads in the capital.
Thousands of BNP leaders, activists and supporters gathered in Nayapaltan from noon. Leaders of the party's associate and affiliated organisations also joined the procession.
The entire Paltan area turned festive with the presence of leaders and activists of the BNP and its associate and affiliated organisations including Jatiyatabadi Sramik Dal, Krishak Dal and Swechchhasebak Dal.
It was Tarique's first participation in a BNP rally since returning to Bangladesh and his first such appearance as the party's chairman.
Earlier in the morning, he paid tribute to BNP founder and former president Ziaur Rahman and former prime minister Khaleda Zia, placing wreaths at their graves at Zia Udyan in Sher-e-Bangla Nagar around 8:30am.
Photo: PMO
The Armed Forces organised special programs, including a display involving 3,000 cadets of the Bangladesh National Cadet Corps and 500 members of Bangladesh Scouts. The Army chief, Air chief, cabinet members, lawmakers, senior government officials and foreign diplomats attended the event.
Various agencies under the home ministry, including Bangladesh Police, Border Guard Bangladesh, Ansar and VDP, the Department of Narcotics Control, Coast Guard, Prisons Directorate and Fire Service and Civil Defence, also arranged milad mahfils, feasts and special darbars.
The BNP is observing the occasion through a seven-day program from November 5 to 11. Alongside the central rally in Dhaka, rallies were held at district and metropolitan levels on Saturday, with further programmes planned at thana and upazila levels on Sunday.
The government also arranged special meals for inmates and residents of hospitals, prisons, orphanages and other state-run institutions. Children were allowed free entry to parks managed by city corporations and municipalities, while educational institutions held discussions and essay competitions.
The Dhaka Elevated Expressway also remained toll-free for all vehicles from 6am to noon on Saturday as part of the observance.

item.title: NCP leaders vandalize signboard at historic home of Language Movement hero Dhirendranath Dutta
item.description:
Leaders of the National Citizen Party (NCP) in Comilla have vandalized a signboard installed at the historic residence of language movement pioneer and martyred freedom fighter Dhirendranath Dutta, triggering widespread debate and mixed reactions on social media.
The incident took place on Friday night at the residence beside Dharmasagar in Comilla city. The NCP leaders said they took the action to prevent the historic property from being sold and to press for its preservation as a national heritage site and conversion into a memorial museum.
Videos showing the signboard being smashed have since gone viral on social media.
The incident has drawn strong condemnation from Aroma Dutta, granddaughter of Dhirendranath Dutta and a former two-time member of parliament from a reserved women's seat.
Local sources said demands for the renovation and preservation of the house, as well as the establishment of a memorial museum, have been raised on several occasions. However, no effective initiative has been taken to implement them.
Recently, Aroma Dutta installed a signboard at the property, claiming ownership through inheritance. She is the daughter of Sanjib Dutta, the only son of Dhirendranath Dutta.
The signboard identified Aroma Dutta as the legal heir and rightful owner of the land. It also mentioned her father's name and the relevant land identification details.
NCP leaders alleged that the property was being prepared for sale and that parts of the old structure had already been removed. Claiming that the signboard was part of an attempt to sell the property, they said they smashed it to prevent the sale of the historic residence.
Eyewitnesses said NCP leaders arrived at the site in the evening and first spoke about the importance of preserving the historic house. They subsequently smashed the signboard installed in front of it.
In a press release issued on Friday night and signed by Comilla Metropolitan NCP Member Secretary Masumul Bari Kawsar, the party described the residence as more than an ordinary building, calling it an important national heritage site closely associated with the Language Movement and the Liberation War.
The statement said the property should not be treated as an object of private commercial transactions and should instead be preserved through a state-led initiative. The party also announced plans to submit written applications to the government and relevant authorities seeking its preservation.
Speaking around 10 pm, Masumul Bari Kawsar said, “We have smashed the signboard to protect a historic house. There is no other motive behind our action.”
He said they hoped the government and Aroma Dutta, as the property's legal heir, would support their initiative.
He also warned that any attempt to sell the land or construct a multi-storey building there would be resisted with the participation of local residents.
Responding to the incident, Aroma Dutta said the property was her ancestral home and that she was its legitimate legal heir, a fact known to the people of Comilla.
“What I decide to do with this property—whether to preserve it or sell it—is entirely my personal matter. But smashing a legally installed signboard at a house in this manner at night is deeply regrettable. I will inform the administration about the incident,” she said.
Officer-in-Charge of Kotwali Model Police Station Touhidul Anwar said police had not yet received any information or complaint regarding the destruction of the signboard.
He added that the matter would be investigated if a complaint was filed.
Dhirendranath Dutta occupies a prominent place in the history of Bangladesh's Language Movement. On February 23, 1948, he made a historic intervention in Pakistan's Constituent Assembly, demanding that Bangla be recognised as a state language alongside Urdu and English.
On the night of March 29, 1971, Pakistani occupation forces abducted him and his son, Dilip Kumar Dutta, from their residence in Comilla. Neither was ever seen again.
In recognition of his outstanding contributions to the Language Movement and the Liberation War, Dhirendranath Dutta was posthumously awarded the Independence Award in 1997.
His granddaughter, Aroma Dutta, served as a member of parliament from a reserved women's seat during the 11th and 12th national parliaments.

item.title: 180 flights to Saudi Arabia cancelled, 23,085 passengers stranded
item.description:
A total of 180 flights from Dhaka to Riyadh and Dammam in Saudi Arabia have been cancelled, leaving 23,085 passengers stranded.
According to sources at the Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh (CAAB), 103 of the flights cancelled between October 10 and November 7 were direct flights, while 77 were transit flights.
Of the direct flights, 51 were operated by Biman Bangladesh Airlines, 10 by US-Bangla Airlines, 21 by Saudia Airlines and 21 by Riyadh Air.
Among the cancelled transit flights, 30 were operated by IndiGo, 14 by Emirates, 9 by Qatar Airways, 8 by flydubai, 7 by SalamAir, 8 by Air India and 1 by EgyptAir.
Kawsar Mahmud, assistant director of the CAAB's Public Relations Division, said flight cancellations would continue if the situation in Saudi Arabia did not return to normal.

item.title: 15 injured in clash between two BNP factions in Brahmanbaria
item.description:
At least 15 people were injured in a clash between two factions of the BNP in Kasba upazila of Brahmanbaria on Saturday afternoon.
The clash broke out in the Kadamtali area of the upazila on November 7, with several crude bombs exploded during the confrontation. The identities of the injured could not be confirmed immediately. They were receiving treatment locally.
According to police and local sources, a procession led by Kasba upazila BNP General Secretary Shariful Haque Swapan was brought out from in front of Araibari Darbar Sharif in the afternoon to mark National Revolution and Solidarity Day. Leaders and activists of the upazila BNP and its affiliated organisations joined the procession.
The procession ended at Kadamtali intersection, where a brief discussion was being held.
At one point, another BNP faction, reportedly loyal to local MP Mushfiqur Rahman, arrived in the area. Tensions between the two groups escalated, triggering a chase and counter-chase that soon turned into a clash.
Both factions reportedly exploded several crude bombs during the confrontation, spreading panic across the area. At least 15 people from the two groups were injured.
Kasba Police Station Officer-in-Charge Ali Md Rashed said the two BNP factions had engaged in a clash, but police later brought the situation under control.
Kasba Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) Samiul Islam said the two factions had organised separate programmes to mark National Revolution and Solidarity Day.
Although both groups had initially assured the authorities that they would hold their programmes peacefully, they later became involved in a clash, he said.
The situation was brought under control through the efforts of law enforcement agencies and is now calm, the UNO added.

item.title: Armed men vandalise another Khulna diagnostic centre
item.description:
Another diagnostic centre in Khulna came under attack on Saturday, as a group of five to six men armed with hammers and Chinese axes stormed the facility and vandalised its premises.
The attack took place at New Apollo Diagnostic and Consultation on Khan Jahan Ali Road in the city around 12:50pm. No casualties were reported.
According to police and local sources, the attackers entered the diagnostic centre carrying hammers and Chinese axes and began smashing equipment and fixtures before anyone could react. They damaged two air conditioners, a television, the glass of the main entrance and the reception counter.
Before carrying out the vandalism, they also snatched a mobile phone worth around Tk30,000 from an employee.
Police visited the scene after being informed of the incident.
Jahid Hossain, manager of the diagnostic centre, said a man claiming to be associated with the Nur Azim gang of Tutpara had called him around a month ago.
“He mentioned Nur Azim, but I told him I did not know the person. The caller then hung up. About a month later, our diagnostic centre came under attack,” he said.
A patient who was at the centre during the incident said all five to six attackers were carrying hammers and Chinese axes.
Khulna Sadar Police Station Officer-in-Charge Lokman Hossain Ripon said police had visited the scene and collected CCTV footage.
“The attackers have been identified by examining the footage. Drives are underway to arrest them,” he said.
The latest incident follows a series of attacks on diagnostic centres in Khulna.
On the night of October 24, Sandhani Diagnostic Centre on Babukhan Road was vandalised and shots were fired, triggering panic among people.
The following day, a group of miscreants went to the second branch of Sandhani Diagnostic Centre in Sonadanga and threatened on-duty doctors at gunpoint.
Abdullah Diagnostic Centre on Shamsur Rahman Road was also attacked on Wednesday.

item.title: Tahsif's death: Dip sent to jail after third round of remand
item.description:
Ahmed Shahriar Reza Dip, described as a ‘friend-like younger brother’ of former air force officer M Tahsif Souri, has been sent to jail after completing his third round of remand in a murder case over Tahsif’s death.
On Saturday, investigation officer Inspector Firoz Uddin of the River Police’s Tongi Outpost produced Dip before the court after the completion of his 10-day remand and sought an order to keep him in jail.
In the remand report, the investigation officer said Dip had provided several important details about the incident during police interrogation. However, the information was being kept confidential pending verification in the interest of the investigation.
The report also described Dip as extremely cunning, saying he had tactfully avoided answering several questions and remained silent during interrogation.
It further stated that Tahsif, Dip and Jerika Tasnim Disha had been seen visiting various places and restaurants together before the incident.
An analysis of CCTV footage, mobile phone call records and other evidence collected so far indicated that Tahsif was last seen with Dip and Disha before his death, suggesting their possible involvement in the incident, the report said.
It added that Dip needed to remain in jail until the investigation was completed to ensure a proper probe, uncover the circumstances surrounding Tahsif’s death and identify and arrest those responsible.
Meanwhile, defence lawyers sought bail for Dip, while the prosecution opposed the plea.
After hearing both sides, Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Md Monirul Islam rejected the bail petition and ordered that Dip be sent to jail.
Saiful Islam, an assistant sub-inspector of the prosecution division, confirmed the matter.
Earlier, the court granted Dip four days of remand on October 31, followed by two successive three-day remand orders on November 3 and 5.
Tahsif went missing on the evening of October 27 after leaving home in response to a call from his junior friend Dip. His body was recovered from the Rajabari Ghat area of the Turag River by River Police the following afternoon.
In connection with his death, Tahsif’s father, KM Enayetul Karim, filed a murder case against unidentified individuals at Uttarkhan Police Station in Dhaka at 1:05am on October 30. Police later showed Dip arrested in the case as a suspect.

item.title: Dhaka roads face traffic congestion over National Revolution Day events
item.description:
Several roads in Dhaka are experiencing traffic congestion on Saturday due to multiple events marking National Revolution and Solidarity Day, with traffic officials advising commuters to avoid affected areas where possible.
The Traffic Division has urged commuters traveling through Manik Mia Avenue, the parliament complex, Tejgaon and surrounding areas to allow extra time for their journeys.
The Ministry of Cultural Affairs is organizing the “Concert for Solidarity” at Manik Mia Avenue. Scheduled to begin at 3pm and continue until midnight, the concert has prompted the closure of 1 lane of the road adjacent to the South Plaza of the National Parliament Building since morning.
A procession is also scheduled to depart from in front of the BNP's central office in Naya Paltan and proceed to the concert venue at Manik Mia Avenue.
As a result, traffic congestion may increase in the afternoon along roads connecting Naya Paltan, Kakrail, Farmgate, Asad Gate and Manik Mia Avenue.
Meanwhile, the Grand Rally of Village Police has been underway since morning at the National Parade Ground in Tejgaon.
Around 40,000 village police personnel are participating in the rally, contributing to traffic congestion around the Trade Fair Ground, Tejgaon and adjacent areas. Traffic disruptions have been reported in these areas since morning.

item.title: Tarique warns of new conspiracies, vows fitting response
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Saturday warned that conspiracies were being hatched against Bangladesh again, saying people would give a fitting response as they had done in the past to protect the country's independence, sovereignty and democracy.
“They were involved in conspiracies in the past, and they are still doing so. Once again, they want to undermine Bangladesh's sovereignty … and bring back the system of 'dummy' elections,” he said.
Tarique made the remarks while speaking briefly before inaugurating a rally marking National Revolution and Solidarity Day in front of the BNP central office at Nayapaltan.
He said no force can suppress the democracy-loving people through conspiracy.
“Just as we did in 1971, in 1990 and on November 7, 1975, we want to give a fitting response again,” Tarique said.
He also called for making the day an occasion to safeguard the democracy that people had established through sacrifice of their lives during the mass uprising on August 5, 2024.
“Let this rally be a day to protect Bangladesh's independence and sovereignty. At the same time, let it be a day to safeguard the democracy that the people of Bangladesh established by sacrificing their lives on August 5, 2024,” the prime minister said.
Seeking the support of thousands of party leaders and activists gathered at Nayapaltan, he asked, “Are you with us?”
The crowd responded with repeated applause.
Tarique called upon people across the country, particularly those who believe in democracy, to stand united against any conspiracy, whether hatched inside or outside Bangladesh.
“Let us, together with all democracy-loving people of Bangladesh, respond to any conspiracy, whether it originates within the country or outside,” he said.
The prime minister warned that no conspiracy would be able to suppress the democratic aspirations of the people.
“November 7 is a day of national unity. It is a day to protect Bangladesh's independence and sovereignty. It is a day of the hopes and aspirations of the people of Bangladesh,” he said.
At the end of his speech, Tarique led the crowd in chanting: “Not Delhi, not Pindi, nor any other country. Bangladesh comes first, Bangladesh for all.”
“Let us begin our revolution today,” he said.
The prime minister said the people of Bangladesh, including students, had not only regained the country's independence and sovereignty but had also driven out the autocratic forces and conspirators.
He said the forces that were defeated on November 7, 1975, had also been defeated through the people's participation in the mass uprising on August 5, 2024.
“The people of a country that achieved independence in 1971, carried out the Sipahi-Janata Revolution on November 7, 1975, and staged the mass uprising in 2024 cannot be kept subdued through conspiracies,” he said.
Tarique arrived at a temporary stage in front of the BNP central office around 3pm and inaugurated the procession marking National Revolution and Solidarity Day.
BNP Standing Committee members Mirza Abbas, Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury, Salahuddin Ahmed and AZM Zahid Hossain, along with Acting Secretary General Ruhul Kabir Rizvi, were among those present on the stage.
Tarique joined the procession on foot, accompanied by cabinet members and leaders from different levels of the party.
The procession reached Manik Mia Avenue around 4:30pm and Tarique delivered the concluding speech there.
Party leaders and activists began gathering at Nayapaltan in small processions from around noon to join the procession.
Thousands of people thronged the area from Kakrail intersection to Fakirerpool, turning the streets into a sea of people.
They carried national flags and placards bearing portraits of BNP founder Ziaur Rahman, former Prime Minister Khaleda Zia and Tarique Rahman. Many wore colourful caps and T-shirts to mark the occasion.

item.title: Senora to run 14 pad dispensers at federations, women's football academies
item.description:
Senora recently became the feminine hygiene partner of Saff's 'Play On Period' project.
The project is an initiative of the AFC Dream Asia Foundation.
Its official pad dispenser was jointly unveiled today at a ceremony at InterContinental Dhaka by Purushottam Kattel, general secretary, Saff; Md Ferdousul Islam, head of media & research, Square Toiletries Limited; and Mahfuza Akter Kiron, AFC executive committee member.
Captains of the national men's football teams of six Saff countries attended the ceremony.
When conversations about menstruation stay limited to women, the taboo is hard to break.
The captains were there to bring male footballers into the conversation. Their presence sent a clear message: breaking the silence around periods is everyone's responsibility.
Under the project, a total of 14 pad dispensers will be installed across Saff's seven member nations, two in each.
The dispensers will be placed at each country's federation headquarters and women's football academies, where female footballers can collect sanitary pads free of charge.
To keep them stocked throughout the year, Senora will ensure a year-long supply of sanitary napkins to all member nations.
In line with the project's goals, coaches, physiotherapists and safeguarding officers will also receive training alongside the dispenser rollout.
Awareness sessions will be organized for female footballers as well.
Earlier on November 1, the first phase of Senora's partnership in the project was completed with the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU).
The ceremony was attended by team managers from six countries, Saff officials, Senora representatives and members of the media.
At the end of the event, the captains, team managers and guests took part in a group photo session.
They then wrote inspiring messages for young girls entering competitive football on the 'Pass the Confidence' board, expressing their solidarity with the Play On Period initiative.

item.title: Abu Lal Group chief arrested with firearms in Habiganj
item.description:
The Detective Branch (DB) of Narsingdi police has arrested Abu Lal, the prime accused in a murder case and leader of the notorious ‘Abu Lal Group’, from Habiganj.
A foreign-made pistol, a magazine and eight rounds of ammunition allegedly used in the murder of Abdullah were also recovered during the operation.
Additional Superintendent of Police (Crime) Ashikur Rahman disclosed the information at a press conference at the police station auditorium on Saturday afternoon.
According to police, Abu Lal had been on the run since Abdullah was killed in the Chowala area of Narsingdi town on October 3.
Police conducted a series of raids in different areas of Narsingdi, Banchharampur and Sadar upazilas of Brahmanbaria, and Dhanmondi in Dhaka to track him down.
He was finally arrested during a raid in Madhabpur upazila of Habiganj on Friday night.
Based on information provided by Abu Lal during preliminary interrogation, police recovered the foreign-made pistol, magazine and eight rounds of ammunition allegedly used in the murder of Abdullah, also known as Babu, on October 2.
A separate case has been filed under the Arms Act over the weapon recovery.
Police said, Abu Lal is in custody and will be produced before a court soon. Efforts are underway to arrest the other fugitives in the case and complete the investigation promptly. Regular patrols and intelligence surveillance have also been stepped up to maintain law and order across the district.

item.title: Kurigram municipal worker killed in front of wife at Nov 7 event
item.description:
A municipal worker was stabbed to death with surgical scissors in front of his wife at Kurigram municipal town hall on Saturday afternoon, shortly after the first session of a programme marking National Revolution and Solidarity Day.
The incident took place at the town hall near College Mor in Kurigram Sadar. The victim’s wife was also injured in the attack and later referred to Rangpur Medical College Hospital for advanced treatment.
The deceased, identified as Mansur, 58, had worked for Kurigram Municipality on a daily-wage basis for years and was serving as the town hall caretaker.
According to officials present at the venue, the suspect, identified as Shahnewaz Sani, 32, entered the town hall after the first session of the programme had ended. Mansur told him that the event was over and there was no need to enter the premises, triggering an argument between the two.
At the time, Mansur’s wife, Mallika, 48, arrived with his lunch. As he was taking the food container from her, the suspect allegedly attacked him repeatedly in the chest with a pair of surgical scissors. When Mallika tried to intervene, she was also attacked.
Other employees rushed to help after hearing their screams and took the injured couple to Kurigram General Hospital, where doctors declared Mansur dead.
Local residents detained the suspect and handed him over to police.
Kurigram Sadar Police Station Officer-in-Charge Kamal Hossain said police had recovered the scissors allegedly used in the attack from the suspect.
The victim’s daughter was preparing to file a case, he said, adding that investigators were examining the motive and why the suspect was carrying the scissors.
“The incident initially appears to have been sudden rather than premeditated,” the OC said.
Deputy Commissioner Annapurna Debnath and officials from the police and municipal administration visited the scene after the incident.
Despite the killing, the second session of the National Revolution and Solidarity Day programme continued at the town hall on Saturday evening.

item.title: Dulu: Path of multi-party politics opened through Ziaur Rahman's leadership
item.description:
Disaster Management and Relief Minister Asadul Habib Dulu on Saturday said the path of a multi-party political system in the country was started through the leadership of BNP founder Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman, paving the way for different political parties to resume their activities.
He made the remarks while addressing a public rally organized by the Lalmonirhat district unit of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), marking National Revolution and Solidarity Day.
The rally began in front of the Bangladesh Nationalist Railway Workers' Union office in the town, marched through major streets, and ended at the same venue, where a public meeting was held.
Dulu said the process of restoring the activities of different political parties began under Ziaur Rahman's leadership, eventually leading to the formation of the BNP on September 1, 1978.
He also said that Ziaur Rahman's political ideals and the party he founded continued to enjoy considerable public support. The BNP, he added, remains committed to establishing people's voting rights, democratic rights and political freedom.
Stressing the importance of public support, Dulu said it was the primary strength of any political party. He called upon all to play responsible roles in strengthening democracy, political rights and national unity to fulfil the aspirations of the people.
Acting general secretary of the district BNP and administrator of the Zila Parishad, AKM Mominul Haque; its joint general secretary, ABM Faruk Siddique; convener of the municipal BNP, Afzal; organizing secretary of the district BNP, Saju Patwary; convener of the district Jubo Dal, Vice President Anis; and its general secretary, Hasan Ali attended the rally, among others.

item.title: DMP urges people not to spread unverified allegations against police
item.description:
Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) has urged people of the country not to circulate unverified allegations against law enforcement agencies on social media without checking the authenticity of any incident.
The appeal came following the circulation of a photograph on Facebook alleging that a woman named Shreemoyee Rita Rani was assaulted by a former leader of Swechhasebak Dal in Mirpur of the capital and police refused to register a complaint over the incident.
In a press release issued on Saturday, DMP said it had reviewed the allegations circulating on Facebook. including a claim by former Chhatra League (now banned) leader SM Zakir that a complaint had been lodged with Mirpur Model Police Station, but police had refused to register a case.
However, an initial inquiry by the Mirpur Division of DMP found no record of any such complaint or case at any of the seven police stations under its jurisdiction, according to the press release signed by Mohammad Akhtar Hossain, deputy commissioner of DMP's Media and Public Relations Division.
Police also found no information indicating that a woman named Shreemoyee Rita Rani had visited any police station under the Mirpur Division to lodge a complaint over the alleged incident.
DMP said it was continuing its investigation to verify the authenticity of the photograph and the allegations, as well as to establish the identity of the woman concerned. However, her exact identity and address have not yet been established, it added.
DMP urged anyone who knows Shreemoyee Rita Rani or has reliable information about her identity, whereabouts or the alleged incident to contact the officer-in-charge of Mirpur Model Police Station or the deputy commissioner of Police (Mirpur Division).
The police said DMP remained committed to ensuring public safety, maintaining law and order and conducting impartial investigations into all complaints.

item.title: Minu urges unity in the spirit of National Revolution and Solidarity Day
item.description:
Land Minister Mizanur Rahman Minu on Saturday called upon people from all walks of life to work together in unity to protect national interests, thwart conspiracies, and advance the country towards prosperity.
He made the call while speaking at a discussion meeting held at the auditorium of Rajshahi District Shilpakala Academy, marking National Revolution and Solidarity Day.
The minister said the people of the country had always demonstrated unity in defending their freedom and sovereignty, from the Liberation War to the recent movement against fascism.
Recalling the Liberation War of 1971, Minu paid tributes to the sacrifices of the East Bengal Regiment and valiant freedom fighters in the Battle of Hili and other frontline battles.
Highlighting the significance of November 7, 1975, he said Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman took responsibility for the country during a critical period, enjoying the trust and support of the common people.
He said Ziaur Rahman inspired farmers, introduced banking facilities for young entrepreneurs, and opened new opportunities for economic emancipation through the introduction of the back-to-back letter of credit system in the readymade garment sector.
The minister also recalled Ziaur Rahman's contributions to enhancing Bangladesh's international dignity, including the planting of neem trees, known as 'Zia Trees', at the Arafat field in Saudi Arabia on behalf of the country.
He paid tributes to Ziaur Rahman's simple lifestyle and former Prime Minister Khaleda Zia's sacrifices in establishing democracy.
Referring to the development of Rajshahi, Minu said the establishment of Rajshahi Metropolitan Police (RMP) had laid the foundation for improving law and order in the region, which had since made significant progress.
He further said Rajshahi had emerged as one of the best medium-sized cities in Southeast Asia, developing into a green, clean and healthy city through the collective efforts of its residents.
Expressing optimism about the city's future, he called for continued unity and collective efforts to sustain the positive trend and take Rajshahi further forward.
Later, the minister distributed prizes among the winners of a painting competition organized to mark National Revolution and Solidarity Day.

item.title: Minister: Nation must be built on the ideals of Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman
item.description:
Agriculture, Fisheries and Livestock Minister Mohammed Aminur Rashid on Saturday called upon BNP leaders and activists at all levels to work in unity, inspired by the ideals and patriotism of Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman.
He said one of the key lessons of "National Revolution and Solidarity Day" is the establishment of national unity.
Embracing this spirit, he said, all should work together under the leadership of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman aiming to make the nation stronger and more prosperous one.
The agriculture minister made the remarks while speaking as the chief guest at a discussion meeting, organised by Comilla South District and City units of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), marking the National Revolution and Solidarity Day.
He said November 7 holds great significance in the history of Bangladesh. Amid various political crises and uncertainties, the uprising of soldiers and the public on this day in 1975 carved a unique place for itself in the nation's history, he said.
Aminur said the core essence of this day is to set aside differences and unite, and this unity must be further strengthened in the national interest.
Speakers at the discussion said the National Revolution and Solidarity Day represents a crucial chapter in the country's political history.
They stressed conveying the significance of this day to the younger generation to uphold the ideals of independence, sovereignty, democracy and national unity.
They also urged the party men to play a responsible role in nation-building and strengthening democratic institutions by following the ideals of Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman.

item.title: Expanding the public transport network
item.description:
The government’s announcement to construct two monorail corridors across the capital by 2030 -- with BUET consultants completing pre-feasibility studies and detailed designs underway -- is certainly a welcome step in expanding Dhaka's public transportation network.
Designed to complement the existing Metro Rail and address last-mile connectivity in high-density bottlenecks, this appears a sensible undertaking to offer a viable, eco-friendly solution to chronic traffic gridlock that only seems to worsen in the capital.
Expanding mass transit has long been an absolute necessity for economic survival in the city, and it is good to see plans being developed to address it.
Yet, public enthusiasm for new transit infrastructure is inevitably tempered by a history of systemic mismanagement, and this apprehension is not without reason.
For decades, Bangladesh’s megaprojects have been plagued by a predictable blueprint of failure: Severe deadline extensions, rampant cost overruns, poor coordination, and opaque procurement processes that balloon into crushing public debts.
When major infrastructure ventures consistently double their original budgets, often as a result of incompetence, disregard, or simple administrative inertia, it is taxpayers who carry that unfair financial burden.
The proposed monorail initiative, and indeed subsequent infrastructure projects, must break decisively from this legacy of inefficiency. If this project suffers the same bureaucratic bloat and inflated expenditures that have tarnished past endeavours, its primary rationale will be completely compromised.
We must thus establish uncompromising governance from day one. The government must set firm, non-negotiable cost caps and strict timeline milestones, holding contractors and public officials accountable for any unjustified delays or financial leakages.
Building modern transit for Dhaka is a crucial step forward and has no alternative. However, it is doing it on time, within budget, and free of corruption that must be ensured.

item.title: There is no prosperity without women’s contribution
item.description:

Women entrepreneurs in particular can do so much more if given a level playing field. Tasking diplomatic missions with helping local women access global markets certainly points toward a visionary ambition, and we welcome it.
Yet, warm words and exhibition showcases will do nothing to alter economic realities unless the state backs them up with radical policy reform.
For decades, small and medium enterprises (SMEs), and particularly women-led businesses, have faced an unforgiving wall of bureaucratic red tape, institutional indifference, and severe financial exclusion.
The harsh reality is that women entrepreneurs across our nation do not merely need diplomatic exposure but need the very basics to operate a business - collateral-free credit, simplified bank loan processing, and protection from predatory lending.
Commercial banks continue to treat women-led SMEs as high-risk ventures, demanding unreasonable collateral and drowning applicants in paperwork. While state agencies draft grand blueprints for export expansion, countless grassroots creators struggle simply to open a basic merchant account or secure working capital.
From operationalizing dedicated, low-interest loan windows specifically tailored for women entrepreneurs to eliminating the bureaucratic hurdles to providing genuine training, digital literacy, and logistical backing for these women, these are just a few ways we can begin to include more women in our journey to economic prosperity.
A trillion-dollar economy cannot be built on the backs of marginalized innovators who are starved of capital and suffocated by red tape. We must move swiftly from policy speeches to concrete financial delivery.
If the government genuinely intends to harness women’s economic potential, structural support must replace empty promises.

item.title: Feeding children is just good economics
item.description:
Economics divides itself into two. Macroeconomics is about how the whole economy works, and it's what we always see the talking heads on TV chattering away about. Inflation, the deficit, interest rates, and so on. Macroeconomics is also the part of economics we don't know much about, and much of what we think we do is wrong.
Microeconomics is the details of prices and markets and interactions between people. Much of what we know here is correct even if many people would prefer that it weren't. For many people would much prefer it if humans didn't go around acting so human all the time.
Those words, macro and micro, also give us a clue. Macro means large, micro small. So, if you want to be a big and important person -- or a talking head on TV -- then you'll want to lean on macroeconomics. You know, chatter on about the big stuff.
But the bit that really makes the difference to how life is lived is that small stuff. As is true in life itself of course -- it's the little things that make life enjoyable and worth living. Further, with micro, we can do experiments and really zero in on what actually works.
The news is that the Bangladeshi government has understood one part of this sort of research and is even doing the right thing about it. It's this : “The government's school feeding initiative is set for a major expansion in 2027, with plans to increase coverage from 3.1 million to around 11 million students at government primary schools across the country.”
We could just say that parents should feed their kids at home and that's that. We could also say that isn't it great that the kids get a lovely meal from the government? But that's not really the point or issue here, it's this: “Ensuring student attendance.”
A lot of research has been done on who sends their kids to school and why. One alarming result was that when child labour is made illegal, then fewer poor children go to school. The logic is that some people are so really poor that any child has to start work so that that child brings in enough money to feed that very same child.
Poor parents know that education is a good thing, it will make the children richer when they're older. But it is necessary for that child to survive long enough to get older.
Research shows that such poor families might well send one or some of the children to school and others have to go to work in order to bring in the necessary money to feed all of them. Of course, it will be more likely to be girls who are made to work while the boys learn to read and write.
If we make child labour illegal, then this will lower the wages the children can receive when working. This is obvious and logical as people will exploit those working illegally more than those working legally. If the wages of the children working fall, more of the children have to work to be able to feed all of the children.
Note that economics is not saying this should happen. It's certainly not approving of it happening. It's just noting that this does happen.
We'd prefer there to be no child labour, of course we would. But as we see, just making it illegal can actually increase the amount of it.
So perhaps we require a different way of achieving our goal?
One of the basic findings of that whole field of microeconomics is that people respond to incentives. In fact, Charlie Munger (he was Warren Buffett's partner) used to say: “Show me the incentive and I'll tell you the outcome.”
Another way of putting that same point is that we should try to tempt people to do the right thing rather than attempt to force them. You know, promising a toddler a sweetie often works better than slapping them in getting them to do something.
So, to restate the poor children and school problem. The parents can only feed the child if the child works, so therefore the child doesn't go to school and is thus trapped in lifelong poverty.
What if we feed the child at school? Then they will both be fed and also be educated? And this time, all the kids can go to school because all the kids will be fed.
This has been studied a lot. There are whole shelves of research in libraries on this. As far as anyone can tell, this works really well.
The World Food Program from the Americans pays for this in many countries and is going to help in Bangladesh. There's also a charity, Mary's Meals, which does the same thing for whole countries. The charity does it possibly better and certainly cheaper than the government, but that's another story.
We've got something that is going to make that future world better. Children will be fed, that's good, but also more children will gain more education.
I personally don't like macroeconomics but a lot of that is because I simply cannot get my head around the advanced mathematics used in it. A failing of mine rather than the subject perhaps.
But I also like this microeconomics because it provides answers to how to make the world a better place in simple, pragmatic, doable ways.
We can just feed every child at school. Feeding every child at school works, makes the world a better place in the future. So, we should do that then.

item.title: What makes growth inclusive?
item.description:
In recent times, there are renewed talks on the notion of inclusive growth. One question that keeps on popping up is what makes growth inclusive.
Everyone agrees that sustained economic growth is central to the ability of countries to advance human development and tackle poverty over a long period of time. But sustained growth alone is not enough to advance human development. For that, growth needs to be inclusive.
Inclusive growth is characterized by three mutually reinforcing elements:
Sustained growth which is pro-poor ensures poverty reduction as well as reduction in inequalities. Equity in resources, services, and income not only leads to human capabilities and opportunities, but it is also crucial for fair and just societies.
When growth is accompanied by rapid increases in productive employment, the incomes of and opportunities for the poor are likely to increase. Productive employment enhances livelihood, participation, dignity, and voice.
All together, inclusive growth is a driving force for human development and the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
To start with sustained growth is a prerequisite for inclusive growth. But sustained growth does not automatically become inclusive. In order to be inclusive, growth has to be pro-poor.
What is pro-poor growth?
The simplest notion of pro-poor growth assumes that so long as growth is associated with a reduction in poverty, it is pro-poor. The problem with this simple definition is that economic growth has largely been found to have some poverty-reducing impacts, at least through its trickledown effects. Thus, in terms of this simple definition, almost all economic growth is pro-poor.
The fundamental point, however, is that the “pro-poorness” of growth is not defined only by its poverty reduction impacts, but by the fact whether the poor actively engage in generating the growth, and also derive disproportionate benefits from it.
In other words, for growth to be pro-poor, the rate of income growth of the poor must exceed the rate of income growth of the non-poor and growth must accompanied by decreasing inequality.
While pro-poor growth is a necessary condition for inclusive growth, it is not a sufficient condition because it may not include non-poor people belonging to ethnic minorities, specific races, and so on. In many cases, these groups of people undertake economic activities which result in good livelihoods, but they have neither a voice in the decision-making process in the mainstream growth, nor are their activities integrated in it.
Equity remains at the heart of inclusive growth as distribution determines the pace, nature, and the pattern of growth. For growth to be inclusive, equity needs to be ensured on three planes:
If the production and the growth process start with an equitable distribution of assets, resources, and endowments, not only would they result in higher growth, but the benefits of growth are also equitably distributed.
When poor farmers have access to land and agricultural input packages, or small-scale entrepreneurs have access to credit, these not only enhance the growth process, but also ensure their fair share in it.
Infrastructure like roads, energy, transport, and communication has an economic activation effect, which implies new economic opportunities, better access to markets, and information. When poor people have access to such infrastructure, it makes growth pro-poor and inclusive.
Equitable access to basic social services, such as health and education and infrastructure, is another central factor for inclusive growth. The theoretical underpinning of this argument can be traced back to Amartya Sen’s work: Development as Freedom .
Inclusiveness effectively means eliminating the various “unfreedoms” experienced by individuals. According to Sen, people’s freedoms are enhanced through the provision of essential social services. Enhancing these freedoms is itself a precondition for achieving inclusive growth. An inclusive growth strategy, therefore, ensures that growth is promoted along with policies that enhance access to social services such as health and education.
In the realm of equity, redistribution of income is also associated with inclusive growth. This works on two fronts.
First , a redistribution of growth benefits the poor through enhancing their income, building their asset base, and enhancing their opportunities -- all of which ensure more inclusion of them in the growth process.
Second , a redistribution of income in various forms of social assistance to marginalized groups (eg, people with disabilities, older people), who cannot participate in the growth process, would provide social protection to them. These people are not part of the generation of growth but still become included in it as beneficiaries.
With regard to equity, two other observations may be pertinent in the context of inclusive growth.
First , equity is also a determining factor of the extent to which economic growth may impact poverty reduction. Initial inequality and changes in inequality are also important factors which can limit the extent to which poor people can participate in and benefit from growth.
Second , gender inequality impacts inclusive growth as well. Gender inequality in education and employment not only has a negative impact on economic growth, but it also adversely affects the pro-poorness of such growth. Also, significant gender gaps in access to agricultural productive assets and input such as land, fertilizer, and modern technologies seriously limit pro-poor growth.
Productive employment is a major driving force for inclusive growth. If growth is to be inclusive, it must be job-creating. This is because productive employment ensures people’s participation in the growth process, both as active agents as well as significant beneficiaries. And poor people can effectively be employed if economic growth is generated in sectors where they are concentrated and if labour-intensive technologies are used.
These linkages remind us of the importance of the sectoral composition of growth. The expansion of capital-intensive mining industries can result in jobless growth, making little impression on poverty. The incomes of the poor largely depend on the nature and extent of employment that economic growth generates.
It basically implies that not all growth is equally employment-intensive and there is no automatic link between economic growth and employment generation. Economic growth can be jobless, as the history of economic development has often shown.
Dr Selim Jahan is Former Director, Human Development Report Office and Poverty Division, United Nations Development Program, New York, USA.

item.title: Middle East could have big role in Democrats’ Trump corruption inquiry
item.description:
Several polls of US voters taken around the recent midterm elections show that an overriding concern about the Trump administration is corruption.
Just days after the midterms, senior figures in the Democratic Party were quick to proclaim that they will be investigating corruption accusations when they take their seats in January.
It’s highly likely that many of those investigations will center on the Trump administration’s and the Trump family’s links to wealthy Middle Eastern countries.
“The incoming Democratic majority in Congress will no doubt aggressively use their powers to investigate the administration’s alleged wrongdoings,” Amy Hawthorne, a non-resident fellow at the Washington-based think tank, the Arab Center, wrote in a commentary after the midterms. “Cases involving the Middle East will be their top targets.”
Financial disclosures made by President Trump in the middle of this year showed that during 2025, his businesses made about $2 billion in income. This was triple the income he reported the previous year, observers noted.
“According to the information available … Middle Eastern countries and businesses have directly contributed to the bottom line of Trump’s family businesses — more so than any other region of the world,” Brian Katulis, a senior fellow and expert in US foreign policy at the Middle East Institute in Washington, wrote in a July text after the presidential disclosure. “Gulf entities paid around $300 million to the president’s businesses in 2025.”
A lot of the money Trump made in 2025 came from the sale of a stake in a cryptocurrency company, World Liberty Financial, Katulis noted.
The company was founded by the Trump and Witkoff families in 2024 — Steve Witkoff is Trump’s special envoy to the Middle East — and in 2025, a large portion of it was sold to an investment firm backed by a senior United Arab Emirates official, Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan. The latter serves as the UAE’s national security advisor and is also the brother of the UAE’s president.
The deal was done in January 2026 behind closed doors, shortly before Trump’s inauguration as president. In May 2026, the US agreed to allow the UAE access to advanced artificial intelligence chips, despite objections from some national security advisers.
Trump’s critics allege a connection; the Trump administration denies it.
There are also other alleged instances of Trump administration corruption with links to the Middle East.
Various Trump deals with Saudi and Emirati real estate developers are also being questioned because of possible conflicts of interest.
The Gulf real estate developers, which have close ties to their governments and respective royal families, have agreed to build Trump-branded golf resorts, hotels, mansions, skyscrapers and towers in Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar and the Maldives.
In 2025, Trump reported $59.5 million in foreign real estate licensing income, ten times more than he made in 2023, business media outlet CNBC reported in August. Nearly two-thirds of that money came from projects in the Gulf, CNBC said.
Ethics watchdogs argue that, “the deals create conflicts between Trump’s political leadership role and private interests” because some of those Gulf states and their developers were also “pursuing major US investments, seeking government permits or pressing for favorable economic and diplomatic relations.”
When the Qatari royal family gifted Trump a luxury jet, worth around $400 million, in May 2025, politicians and ethics experts asked about the propriety of taking such a pricey present from a foreign government.
After his presidency ends, Trump was apparently planning to donate the plane to his Florida-based project, the Donald J Trump Presidential Library Foundation. Currently, it is unclear whether the Qatari plane will end up there and there’s been speculation Trump will try to keep it for personal use.
The library is a non-profit and has received tens of millions in funding — an investigation by the CBS network traced over $100 million in donations — from lawsuits and via corporate donors.
Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren has already said the library project would be investigated. “Giant corporations and foreign governments should not be able to buy influence in Washington with donations to the president’s library,” she told CBS.
Plans for the so-called Board of Peace were created in September 2025 and the body was to facilitate a ceasefire and reconstruction in Gaza.
It was set up to be a kind of multilateral international organization, similar to the United Nations, except that Trump would serve as its chairman indefinitely and member countries donating $1 billion if they want to sit on the board permanently.
The Board of Peace has not achieved much in Gaza, experts say, and there have been several worrying developments.
Four months after its establishment, the World Bank account set up to manage Board of Peace funds was empty, the Financial Times newspaper reported in May. Instead, money had been deposited into a private JP Morgan bank account, over which there was no oversight.
There have apparently been contributions of around $3 million from Morocco and $20 million from the UAE, as well as pledges of $7 billion from board members and $10 billion from Trump.
The board’s legal status was also changed to make it into an international non-governmental organization. This change in legal status may aim “to avoid US congressional oversight and keep much of its activity opaque,” Zaha Hassan, an attorney and senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, warned in a June commentary. It also “gives Trump ultimate decision-making authority, including over financial matters,” she noted.
“The Trump crime family is the top of our investigative priorities,” the most senior Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, Robert Garcia, said after the midterms.
And he has already expressed concerns about the behavior of Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner in the Middle East.
Most of the issues around Kushner involve potential conflicts of interest. Kushner is acting as a volunteer envoy in the Middle East and has been deeply involved in negotiations to end the Gaza conflict and the Iran war.
In early October, CNN published an investigation that detailed links between Kushner’s private equity company, Affinity Partners, and investments into leading Israeli military manufacturers.
It’s also been reported that while he was travelling in the region, Kushner was trying to raise billions for his equity firm.
In March, Democratic politicians, including Garcia, wrote letters to the president’s office, saying they had “serious concerns about whether the White House is letting Mr Kushner use his influence for personal financial gain.”
The potentially most damaging claims against Kushner come from a recent book, “Prince and Thieves,” published late October by American investigative journalist Matthew Cole.
Cole alleges, “Kushner worked with the UAE to shape US policy across the Middle East and that, in the course of this work, he was given access to bank accounts containing roughly $2 billion,” the New York Times wrote in its review.
Kushner denies the allegations about any such slush fund held by an Israeli bank and has threatened to sue Vanity Fair magazine, which published excerpts from the book.
But, as the New York Times concluded, “Cole’s work is sufficiently calm, detailed and forensic to necessitate a large-scale and urgent congressional inquiry.”

item.title: New Zealand’s political future in the balance as main parties slump
item.description:
New Zealand’s political future was in the balance on Saturday with over two-thirds of votes counted and both major parties needing to form coalitions to govern after a campaign dominated by worries over rising costs of living and the economy.
Kiwis are struggling to make ends meet -- the price of basic goods remains stubbornly elevated, and unemployment at its highest in more than a decade.
The war in the Middle East and the subsequent global fuel shock have been widely blamed for the hit to New Zealand’s economy.
With over two-thirds of votes counted, neither the conservative National Party nor the center-left Labor will have enough seats in parliament to govern without help from minor parties.
The two main parties are neck and neck at 29%, with just a few thousand votes separating them.
“New Zealand has spoken. It may take us a little bit longer to figure out exactly what it is that you’ve said,” Labor leader Chris Hipkins told supporters.
“Our next parliament is going to require all of us to compromise, to work together, and to find common ground.”
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon had hoped his right-wing coalition could cling to power with promises of “no new taxes,” after three fractious years in office, two failed bids by his own party to oust him as leader and an economy in the doldrums.
And while his National have a path to power and the largest number of seats, they would do so without several of their most senior and highest-performing members.
Deputy leader and Finance Minister Nicola Willis will not return to parliament due to her party’s poor performance in party voting.
And Chris Bishop, the minister for housing, infrastructure and transport, looks set to lose his Hutt South seat, leaving him out of parliament.
The knife-edge poll drew intense attention on the country’s minor parties, in particular the upstart centrist Opportunity Party.
Under the country’s mixed-member proportional representation (MMP) system, voters must tick two options -- a general party list as well as an individual member to represent their electorate.
Results put Opportunity winning over five percent -- the threshold needed to gain seats in parliament without an electorate candidate win, which would likely secure the party a kingmaker role in the next government.
The party is led by former KPMG consultant Qiulae Wong, who has vowed a kinder, gentler politics and said she could work with whichever party wins the most seats.
“You guys have voted for unity over division,” she said as votes rolled in.
“You have voted to change New Zealand politics for good.”
At a Labor event bedecked with red balloons in Upper Hutt, near Wellington, party workers were quietly confident they had secured the largest number of seats.
Hipkins arrived late to cheers of “Chippy” -- greeted with adulation even as he accepted that Labor may not play a role in the next government.
And at a National gathering in the country’s largest city of Auckland, Finance Minister Willis was hugged and heralded by supporters as she effectively conceded she had been ousted.
“It’s pretty much exactly what we thought it was going to be, really, really tight race,” Immigration Minister and National lawmaker Erica Stanford said.
“It’s a really sad night,” she added, paying tribute to her ousted cabinet colleague.

item.title: Iran says forces ‘stronger’ than at beginning of war
item.description:
Iran said Saturday its military has grown “stronger” since the outset of its war with the United States, which has offered a $20 million reward for information about Tehran’s nuclear program.
Mediators have been working to prevent any resumption of fighting after months of deadlock in the Middle East conflict, which began when the United States and Israel attacked Iran in late February.
Tehran has sought to limit traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, which normally carries about one-fifth of global oil consumption.
Iranian army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia said Tehran retained control over the strategic waterway and that it would remain closed until its demands were met by the United States.
He also said Iran’s forces had grown stronger and more confident, state news agency IRNA reported on Saturday.
“Today, the Islamic Republic’s armed forces... having gained experience from direct confrontation with the United States and the Israeli regime, are on higher alert and are stronger than they were at the beginning of the war,” he said.
“They now possess greater motivation, commitment, and self-confidence.”
“Under the order of the Supreme Leader, the response of the armed forces will be immediate, effective, and without geographical limitations,” he added.
On Friday, the US military said it was offering a $20 million reward “and possible relocation” for information about Iran’s nuclear program.
Rewards for Justice, a State Department program, was seeking information on topics including “facilities, equipment, and associated personnel, such as those in the scientific community,” US Central Command said on X.
The program was established in 1984 under the State Department’s national security rewards program to offer money for information that protects American lives and interests.
In a statement about the reward, the State Department said Iran’s “lack of compliance with the (International Atomic Energy Agency) on safeguards obligations has led to the agency’s loss of ‘continuity of knowledge’ regarding Iran’s production and inventory of key components like centrifuges.”
It did not specify what type of information would warrant a $20 million reward.
US President Donald Trump has repeatedly said US forces have effectively obliterated Iran’s nuclear program.
“If we didn’t hit Iran, you wouldn’t have Israel today,” Trump said Friday night in West Palm Beach, Florida.
“If they had nuclear, they would have used nuclear. They would have obliterated the Middle East.”
The president also said Iran -- which he stressed has had its economy and military severely damaged over eight months of war -- is eager to end the conflict.
“We’re dealing with them now. They want to make a deal very badly,” he said.
Trump called Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani on Friday to discuss efforts to end the war.
Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian said this week his government was still trying to resolve the crisis through dialogue.
Early on Saturday, Iran’s Tasnim news agency reported that two missiles had struck Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, adding there was no official information about any damage.
Iranian state television reported two explosions on the island.
The Iranian army said early Saturday that its air defenses had “struck and destroyed” a US drone that was flying over the island, according to state media. It did not say whether the island was attacked.

item.title: France braces for protests as Yellow Vests urge ‘mass disobedience’
item.description:
French unions and student groups are set to take to the streets for another day of protests on Saturday, while the Yellow Vests movement plans a separate rally in central Paris despite a ban by authorities.
The demonstrations follow weeks of youth-led unrest and nationwide strikes that drew hundreds of thousands of workers protesting the rising cost of living.
They come less than six months before voters elect a new head of state to replace centrist President Emmanuel Macron, with the far right leading in opinion polls.
Student groups and trade unions have called for an authorized march in central Paris “against the high cost of living and in support of young people.”
Yellow Vests activists, however, have refused to join, instead calling for a separate rally at Place de la Concorde, near the lower house of parliament and presidential palace, despite a ban by authorities on demonstrations in the area.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said 70,000 police officers and security forces would be deployed across the country.
“If there are any rioters or looters... we’ll be ready and waiting for them,” he said.
The demonstrations have been largely peaceful, but there have at times been clashes with police or vandalism on their sidelines, including on October 17, when France saw its worst rioting in years.
On Thursday, hundreds of thousands of striking workers took to the streets across France in mostly orderly protests, although clashes between demonstrators and police broke out in several cities.
The Yellow Vests movement, which gained traction eight years ago with huge grassroots protests against Macron’s government over planned fuel-tax hikes, has called for its banned rally to go ahead.
“We are calling for mass disobedience,” said Benjamin Ball, a member of its coordinating committee.
Authorities are determined to prevent a repeat of the rioting and looting that marred the October 17 demonstrations, although the interior ministry said Thursday’s protests had “generally gone well” despite 642 arrests.
The police response has faced criticism for being heavy-handed, with dozens of internal investigations launched into allegations of brutality against demonstrators.
After several instances of apparent police brutality against AFP reporters covering the protests, the international news agency on Friday urged protection for its journalists.
Press freedom watchdog Reporters Without Borders (RSF) said it had recorded 40 cases of journalists being obstructed in their coverage of the demonstrations by members of the security forces, including 21 cases involving physical violence.
Macron’s government is grappling for responses to the protests as he approaches the end of his presidency in May 2027.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu is due to discuss wages and purchasing power with representatives of trade unions and employers’ organizations on Monday.
“The only thing that will bring the protests to an end is a response to the demands that have been put forward for several weeks by workers, civil servants, young people and pensioners,” an inter-union coalition said on Friday.
The unions are calling for an increase in the minimum wage, which has not received any discretionary boost since 2012, across-the-board wage raises, tax reforms and better learning conditions for young people.
With the European Union’s second-largest economy under pressure to rein in debt, the government has limited scope to appease protesters.

item.title: BRAC University hosts 2nd int'l conference on language studies
item.description:
The second International Conference on Epistemic Reconfigurations in Language Studies (ERLS) began on Friday, 6 November 2026, at BRAC University’s main campus in Merul Badda, Dhaka, bringing together more than 250 scholars, practitioners and students to examine language, knowledge production and the impact of historical and colonial legacies.
Organized by the BRAC Institute of Languages (BIL), the two-day conference features 145 presentations, three keynote sessions, two invited speakers, two ‘Rising Stars’ and three colloquium sessions, with participants from Bangladesh and abroad.
Addressing the inaugural ceremony, Professor Dr Mamun Ahmed, chairman of the University Grants Commission of Bangladesh and chief guest, highlighted the importance of multilingual communication in an increasingly interconnected world.
He said learning another language could create opportunities for education, employment, cultural exchange, research collaboration and stronger international relations.
Lulzim Pllana, who attended as the guest of honor, said communication across languages and cultures, along with the exchange of ideas and perspectives, would be essential to building a more connected and collaborative future.
Professor Dr Arshad Mahmud Chowdhury, pro-vice-chancellor of BRAC University and chair of the inaugural ceremony, emphasized the importance of recognizing intellectual traditions and knowledge from the Global South.
He said knowledge and academic practices from the Global North had long been treated as primary sources of authority, while the languages, histories and experiences of the Global South had often received less recognition. He added that decolonial thinking encouraged people to question established assumptions and create space for diverse perspectives.
In her welcome speech, Lady Syeda Sarwat Abed, advisor and founder of BIL, said language education should be inclusive, relevant and transformative while remaining connected to learners' cultural and social contexts.
Professor Shaila Sultana, director of BIL and convenor of ERLS, said the institute was expanding language education beyond traditional classrooms through practical programs, including communication workshops for healthcare workers and nurses, as well as language labs to support safer migration.
The conference features three keynote speakers: Dr David Block of Universitat Pompeu Fabra, Spain; Dr Ana Deumert of the University of Cape Town, South Africa; and Professor Peter I De Costa of Michigan State University, USA.
The invited speakers are Professor Yongyan Zheng of Fudan University and Dr Anwar Ahmed of the University of British Columbia, Canada. The ‘Rising Stars’ segment features Dr Nasrin Pervin of North South University and Mohammad Mosiur Rahman of the University of Liberal Arts Bangladesh.

item.title: Police come under attack during AL procession in Chittagong
item.description:
Police came under attack during a procession by the activities-banned Awami League in the Bandar area of Chittagong city on Friday, with 20 people arrested in connection with the incident.
Six police personnel, including Bandar police station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Abdur Rahim, were injured in the incident, which took place around 3pm in the Taltala area of Port Connecting Road under Bandar police station.
According to police and local sources, leaders and activists of the activities-banned Awami League brought out a procession in the area on Friday afternoon. After receiving information about the procession, a police team went to the scene and attempted to stop it.
At that point, participants allegedly threw brickbats at police and smashed the glass of a police vehicle, injuring 6 police personnel, including the OC.
Police later chased the procession participants and arrested 20 people from the scene.
A case has been filed with Bandar police station over the attack on police under the Anti-Terrorism Act.
OC Abdur Rahim said brickbats were thrown at police during the procession and the glass of a police vehicle was smashed. He added that police operations to arrest the other participants were continuing.
